Configure your server

Sign-in and accounts

Choose who can create an account and how people sign in: allowlists, email verification, SSO, passkeys and password rules.

Who can sign up

SIGNUPS_ENABLED=true
SIGNUP_ALLOWLIST=you@example.com,@company.com

SIGNUPS_ENABLED and SIGNUP_ALLOWLIST come from the operator’s environment on every start. An empty allowlist clears any old stored list; signup order never grants privileges.

Server configuration belongs in the operator’s environment. App accounts cannot change signup policy, server integration credentials, or deployment updates, and cannot read deployment security logs.

There is no app-admin role, first-user privilege, or ADMINS list. Workspace owners manage only their own workspace.

RAKAZO_ADMIN_EMAILS names accounts, comma-separated, that review plugin submissions, add stdio MCP servers (integrations), and, on deployments that sell model credits, give free access at /admin/access. An account counts only once its email is verified. It grants nothing else.

A free-access grant names an email and gives up to $1,000 of model credits, up to 12 free own-key months, or both. Whoever owns an organization with that verified email receives it the next time they open the app, whether they signed up before or after the grant. A grant can be revoked until it is received.

Email verification and sign-in codes

With a nonempty signup allowlist and SMTP configured, users—including existing accounts—must verify their email to sign in. Without an allowlist, verification never blocks: a password signup signs in at once and is sent a verification link that only marks the address verified.

SMTP also enables sign-in with a six-digit emailed code, which expires after ten minutes and allows three attempts. A code can create an account, so it follows the same registration and allowlist rules as password signup. Signing in with a code to an existing unverified account removes that account’s password, SSO links and sessions, since nothing proved they belonged to the mailbox owner. This is what stops someone who registered another person’s address from keeping access. A password reset proves the mailbox the same way, so resetting an unverified account’s password also removes its SSO links, passkeys and paired devices.

Allowlisted signup requires mailbox verification and email delivery, including the first account. Without email delivery, use the server-side account bootstrap described below; public signup never marks an address verified or assigns server permissions.

Installations without email

For an installation without email, first set SIGNUPS_ENABLED=false in .env and start the stack. Create the intended account privately (the password stays in the shell environment):

read -r -p "Account email: " OWNER_EMAIL
read -r -s -p "Account password (at least 16 characters): " OWNER_PASSWORD
export OWNER_EMAIL OWNER_PASSWORD
docker compose --env-file .env -f docker-compose.images.yml exec -e OWNER_EMAIL -e OWNER_PASSWORD api node dist/cli/bootstrap-owner.js
unset OWNER_EMAIL OWNER_PASSWORD

For a source checkout, use -f infra/compose/docker-compose.yml instead. This creates an ordinary verified account and a personal workspace, with no server privileges. For an existing unverified account, its password must match before it can be verified; an existing verified account is left unchanged. Keep an installation without email on a trusted local network.

Verification and password recovery email

Password changes for signed-in users require no email configuration. Forgotten-password recovery appears on sign-in only when a transactional email provider is available. WhatEverFi uses a provider-neutral contract with Resend API and SMTP adapters. Templates render locally with React Email into HTML and plain text, independent of the sending provider.

To use the Resend HTTP API, verify a sending domain and create a sending-only API key restricted to that domain, then configure:

EMAIL_PROVIDER=resend
EMAIL_API_KEY=replace-with-sending-api-key
EMAIL_FROM=WhatEverFi <hello@mail.example.com>

Disable click and open tracking for account email in the provider’s domain settings. Resend delivery has a ten-second deadline and bounded retries with the same idempotency key, including when a response is lost. Errors omit provider response bodies and credentials.

For Amazon SES or another SMTP server, use:

SMTP_URL=smtps://smtp-user:replace-with-password@smtp.example.com:465
EMAIL_FROM=WhatEverFi <no-reply@example.com>

Set EMAIL_REPLY_TO to send replies somewhere other than EMAIL_FROM.

EMAIL_PROVIDER=smtp is optional: an existing SMTP_URL continues to select SMTP when no provider is specified. EMAIL_PROVIDER=none disables external sending. Explicit provider settings take precedence over an old SMTP_URL; incomplete or unknown provider configurations fail at startup.

Resend also supports SMTP: use smtp.resend.com, username resend, and an API key as the password. For Amazon SES, use the regional SMTP endpoint and SES SMTP credentials; these are different from ordinary AWS access keys. Verify the sender/domain with the provider before testing delivery. Keep credentials in .env, never in tracked files. smtps:// uses implicit TLS; smtp:// is also supported but requires STARTTLS. WhatEverFi rejects configuration that disables TLS or certificate verification.

Local source development can use the offline email emulator instead. It captures email without contacting a provider:

EMAIL_EMULATOR=true

The emulator is forcibly disabled when NODE_ENV=production and requires the API to bind to a loopback host. In NODE_ENV=development, captured messages are available from http://127.0.0.1:3100/api/dev/emails with cache disabled; the API logs only delivery metadata, never reset tokens. The inbox route is not registered in test, staging, or production.

Set WELCOME_EMAIL_ENABLED=true to send each new account one welcome email, with an unsubscribe link, after it first signs in. It needs one of the providers above.

Password policy

New passwords (signup, reset and change) must be 8 to 128 characters, with no composition rules. Optionally reject new passwords that appear in known breaches:

AUTH_BREACHED_PASSWORD_CHECK_ENABLED=true

This queries the Have I Been Pwned range API, sending only the first five characters of the password’s SHA-1 hash. It is off by default so the server makes no outside request. If the service is unreachable or takes longer than three seconds, the password is accepted and the failure logged.

OpenID Connect SSO

SSO works with a self-hosted or hosted OpenID Connect provider. Leave its settings unset to keep password authentication alone. Configure all three credentials together on the API:

OIDC_ISSUER=https://identity.example.com
OIDC_CLIENT_ID=replace-with-client-id
OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET=replace-with-client-secret
OIDC_NAME=SSO
OIDC_SCOPES=openid email profile
AUTH_PASSWORD_ENABLED=true
OIDC_ALLOW_SIGNUP_BYPASS=false

The issuer must be HTTPS and exactly match the discovery document’s issuer. WhatEverFi loads <issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration, verifies ID tokens against discovery JWKS with issuer, audience and nonce checks, and uses authorization codes with PKCE. Additional scopes may be space- or comma-separated; openid email profile are always requested. OIDC_NAME is the button label, defaulting to “SSO”. Secrets remain on the API; Compose clears the worker’s OIDC credentials. The capabilities endpoint exposes only the label, discovery availability, and enabled authentication methods.

Register this redirect URI at the provider (using your public BETTER_AUTH_URL origin):

https://app.example.com/api/auth/callback/oidc

Web, Electron and mobile use the same provider redirect URI. Electron completes SSO in a sandboxed in-app popup sharing the app’s session, then returns to the main window. Mobile completes the callback on the API, then returns to rakazo://sign-in (or rakazo://account for linking and reauthentication) through Better Auth’s Expo authorization proxy and a native auth browser session. The rakazo app scheme is trusted by the auth server; never register a client secret in the mobile app. Mobile stores the resulting session with SecureStore, like password sign-in. Native builds need the Expo WebBrowser module.

Provider emails are verified only when email_verified is the boolean true. False or missing claims stay unverified, including on subsequent sign-ins, and an unverified claim never changes the account’s email. Sign-in never links accounts by email, except to claim an account directory provisioning created. If an email belongs to another account, sign in to that existing account and choose Link SSO in account settings. Linking requires an authenticated session, a verified provider email and matching email addresses. With email delivery, an account links SSO only after its email is verified. Without it, an unverified account links only from a browser signed in to it, so not from the mobile app. The issuer and provider subject identify the linked account thereafter. Changing issuers does not reuse an old identity. Old-issuer links remain stored but do not count as linked to the current provider, so Link SSO becomes available again. Link the new identity from the existing signed-in account; authenticated-session, verified-email and matching-email checks still apply. Restoring the old issuer makes its existing links usable again.

Ordinary SSO sign-in and linking may reuse the identity provider’s existing session. They do not grant fresh authentication proof for account deletion. The account settings’ explicit reauthentication flow requests prompt=login and max_age=0, binds the callback to the same linked issuer and subject, and requires the initiating session to remain valid. Only that callback grants proof to the resulting session, expiring five minutes after provider authentication (callback delays do not extend it). Its verified ID token must contain an auth_time consistent with that request (allowing 60 seconds of clock skew) and less than five minutes old. Missing, stale or invalid claims fail closed. OAuth callbacks are single-use, including concurrent requests. Password verification and emailed deletion codes remain available. Submit deletion codes through the account settings or the CSRF-protected POST /api/auth/delete-user endpoint; the GET deletion callback is disabled.

SSO signup follows closed registration and the deployment allowlist before creating an account. Allowlisted provider emails must be verified; signup never bypasses mailbox proof. OIDC_ALLOW_SIGNUP_BYPASS=true explicitly admits IdP identities without applying the allowlist or its email-verification admission requirement. Enable it only when the IdP controls who may join this deployment. It does not reopen closed registration, and does not change email verification claims or linking rules. Existing admitted accounts can sign in while registration is closed.

Set AUTH_PASSWORD_ENABLED=false for SSO-only operation. Password sign-in, signup, password reset and password mutation endpoints are disabled server-side, and sign-in forms are hidden. The API refuses to start in this mode unless all OIDC credentials are configured. It can still start while discovery is temporarily unavailable: the provider remains registered, sign-in returns a temporary error, and background retries recover without restarting. Discovery is lazy on first use, refreshed in the background, and failures back off up to one minute. Availability reflects discovery, not a guarantee that the provider’s token endpoint is currently reachable.

Account deletion keeps the existing password confirmation for password users. Users without a password may delete after explicit provider reauthentication within five minutes; Sign in again starts a fresh provider round-trip bound to the signed-in account. Choosing a different identity cannot confirm deletion or create another account in that flow. A stale or borrowed session alone cannot authorize deletion. With transactional email configured, Send deletion code sends a single-use code to the account email, valid for ten minutes. Enter it in account settings to confirm deletion. Email-code requests are rate-limited; invalid, expired or wrong-account codes fail. No password needs to be created for deletion.

Directory provisioning (SCIM)

Your identity provider can add people to WhatEverFi and remove them over SCIM 2.0. Generate a token (openssl rand -hex 32) and set it on the API:

SCIM_BEARER_TOKEN=<your generated token>

In the identity provider, set the SCIM base URL to https://app.example.com/api/auth/scim/v2 (your BETTER_AUTH_URL origin) and the bearer token to that value. The token manages users only; group requests are refused. Rotating it means changing the value and restarting the API.

  • Adding a person creates an account with their email, unverified, and no password. It joins WhatEverFi even while signup is closed or the allowlist would refuse it, so SIGNUPS_ENABLED=false with SCIM admits exactly the people the directory assigns. They sign in through SSO (the first SSO sign-in with the same verified email claims the account) or with an emailed sign-in code.
  • A person who already has an account keeps it: the directory takes it over by email without changing its name, email or logins, and can then turn it off. Only an account whose email was verified is taken over. Anyone could have signed up first with an address nobody proved, so the directory gets a conflict for it, as it does when two accounts’ emails differ only by case; the operator decides what to do with those accounts.
  • Turning a person off (active: false) or deleting them deactivates the account at once. It ends every sign-in and paired computer, removes notification registrations, cancels runs they started, skips their routines, and refuses any new sign-in, run, webhook delivery or message from their linked chat apps. Their bots, chats, memory, files and connections stay. They also leave every shared space someone else invited them into, as if removed: what they made there passes to that space’s owner, and their routines there are paused. Spaces they own stay theirs. Turning them back on restores sign-in and their own spaces, and routines there resume from their next scheduled time. Shared spaces they left need a new invite.
  • Adding a deleted person again with the same external id finds their existing account.

Without an identity provider, the operator can do the same from the API container:

docker compose --env-file .env -f docker-compose.images.yml exec api \
  node dist/cli/account-status.js deactivate person@example.com   # or reactivate

While SCIM_BEARER_TOKEN is set, it leaves accounts the identity provider manages to the provider: it will not turn off one the provider has on, or turn back on one the provider turned off or deleted. Once the token is removed, it changes any account. The same command finishes a deactivation whose cleanup failed. Sign-in and runs are refused as soon as the account is off, and the API logs directory.account_change.unfinished with the account id if ending its sessions, computers or runs did not complete.

Deactivation and reactivation are recorded as auth.account.deactivated and auth.account.reactivated security events and in each of the person’s organizations’ audit log. The directory never deletes an account or its content.

Passkeys

Passkeys are on whenever WEB_ORIGIN is an HTTPS domain (or localhost in development); the relying party is that origin’s host, so existing passkeys keep working only while WEB_ORIGIN stays on the same domain. They are off when password sign-in is disabled for SSO-only deployments. On web, a browser offers them where it has a platform authenticator. The macOS desktop app uses the system passkey sheet, which only serves the domain the release is associated with (app.whateverfi.com), so it hides passkeys for other servers.

Native apps can use a domain’s passkeys only when the domain vouches for them and the app was built for that domain. The iOS app’s associated domain comes from EXPO_PUBLIC_API_URL at build time. A macOS desktop build takes it from RAKAZO_PASSKEY_RP_ID (default app.whateverfi.com): set it to the same domain for pnpm build and for scripts/passkey-entitlements.ts, then package with electron-builder’s -c.mac.entitlements set to that script’s output and -c.mac.provisioningProfile set to a profile for your App ID with the Associated Domains capability, as the release workflow does. Without both, macOS ignores the association and the app hides passkeys. When Apple’s CDN cannot reach the server (a private network or a VPN such as Tailscale), also set RAKAZO_PASSKEY_DEVELOPER_MODE=1 for either build: a development-signed app then fetches the association file itself, once associated-domains developer mode is on (Settings > Developer on iOS, sudo swcutil developer-mode -e true on macOS, where the app must also live in /Applications). To let a build use this server’s passkeys, set:

# iOS and the macOS desktop app (dev.rakazo.desktop): <Apple Team ID>.<bundle id>, comma-separated.
# Served as /.well-known/apple-app-site-association.
PASSKEY_APPLE_APP_IDS=ABCDE12345.com.rakazo.app,ABCDE12345.dev.rakazo.desktop
# Android: SHA-256 fingerprints of the app signing certificates, comma-separated.
# Served as /.well-known/assetlinks.json and accepted as passkey origins.
PASSKEY_ANDROID_CERT_SHA256=AA:BB:...:FF

Until a platform’s setting is set, the native app on that platform hides passkeys for this server. Both files are served through the web origin, so a reverse proxy in front of the web container must pass /.well-known/ through to it.
